agree.reason: The email makes a polite case on the editor's own sales record, but an editor with a $9,000 budget and an $8,000 newer illustrator gets no reason to pay $2,500 more: it offers nothing extra (spot drawings, a sketch date, a September 1 guarantee) and doesn't say Elena can't do the book at $9,000.

honest.reason: Every figure matches the brief, the unsupported claim that every other publisher pays at least $12,000 is rightly left out, and "lower half of that range" holds because $11,500 is below the $12,000 midpoint.

works_the_facts.reason: It repeats the facts but derives nothing from them: no note that the fee hasn't moved across six books in four years, no monthly figure (about $2,250 a month for four months' work), and no mention of the fourth printing, so the sales record carries less weight than it could.

right_comparison.reason: The $12,500 fee and the agent's range give an outside benchmark, but the editor's real alternative, a less proven illustrator at $8,000, is never compared against Elena's record of two titles over 20,000 copies and reliable delivery.

qualification.reason: A checkable commitment with dates would strengthen this ask, such as sketches within 6 weeks of signing, final art by September 1 and an answer by the end of next week, but the email gives no dates or terms at all.

objections.reason: The obvious objections (the budget is $9,000, and someone cheaper is available) go unanswered: there are no added extras, no delivery guarantee and no clear floor, and "lower half of the range" does only a little to address cost.

fit.reason: It is a well-toned email of about 190 words, under the 250 limit, but it has a generic subject and greeting, no sign-off name, and never names The Night Garden or Nadia.
